title: About
paragraph1: People are taught to pick a lane early and build everything around it. I've always thought that leaves too much on the table. Think of Leonardo da Vinci: a polymath, a man of both science and art, the very symbol of the Renaissance ideal. There's a reason that model still resonates: breadth isn't a distraction, it's how you see things other people miss.
paragraph2: In practice, it's meant moving from engineering into marketing and SEO, and eventually into building the automations that hold those worlds together. I spent years inside an agency watching good work get buried under spreadsheets nobody fully trusted and manual steps nobody had time to fix. So I started fixing them, and it turned out that was the most interesting work in the room.
paragraph3: I'm good at seeing how everything connects, and I tend to care more about the business problem than the technical one. The question I always end up at is: what is this person spending time on that they really shouldn't have to? When the answer is clear, everything else follows.
